title: Asalha again
hookLine: the first sermon, heard a third year

lines: FIVE ASCETICS IN THE DEER PARK.
WE WON'T STAND UP FOR HIM.
cards: Five wandering ascetics are camped in the Deer Park near Benares. They used to practice with Gotama, until he gave up the harsh fasting and they left him in disgust.

Now one of them spots a familiar figure walking up the path. It's him. The Vinaya says they make a pact on the spot: we won't stand up for him, we won't take his bowl, we'll just leave a seat out in case he wants to sit.
He keeps walking toward them. Today, for the Asalha full moon, what happened next, a third time.

teach.b: First, the pact breaks. As he comes closer, they can't keep it. One takes his bowl and robe, one sets out a seat, one brings water for his feet.
The text says simply that they were not able to keep it.

The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, the Setting in Motion of the Wheel of the Teaching, opens with two extremes, in paraphrase: a life given over to sense pleasure, low and unprofitable, and a life given over to self-torment, painful and unprofitable.
He had tried both. Between them runs a middle way.

Third, the four truths, the heart of the sermon. There is suffering: birth, aging, sickness, death, being with what you don't love, losing what you do. Suffering has a cause: craving, the thirst that keeps reaching.
Suffering can end, when that craving fades and is let go. And there's a way to that ending, the noble eightfold path. Fourth, the listener.

As the Buddha spoke, the sutta says, one of the five, Kondanna, saw it clearly: whatever has the nature to arise has the nature to cease. Some readers hear that short line as the whole sermon folded small.

Why hear it a third time? Because the sutta isn't only an event in a park. In the Theravada tradition, the Asalha full moon keeps it alive every year, and the wheel is said to have been set rolling, not finished.
It turns again each time someone hears it.

how: On Asalha Puja, Theravada Buddhists visit temples to hear the first sermon recited or explained, make offerings, and in some places walk around the temple with candles; the rains retreat begins soon after.

o: a festival marking the end of the rains
the full moon of the Buddha's passing away
the full moon recalling the first sermon

games.q: the wheel, again: tap the pairs.
p: agreed not to rise or take his bowl
craving, the thirst that keeps reaching

s: the five ascetics kept their pact and ignored him
as he came closer, they couldn't keep it: bowl taken, seat set, water brought.
the first sermon names two extremes before the middle way
sense pleasure and self-torment, both called unprofitable.
the sermon says suffering can never end
the third truth: suffering can end, when craving fades and is let go.

games.q: you're one of the five. you agreed not to greet the man who gave up fasting. now he's at the edge of your camp. what happens?
o: you keep the pact and look away
you find yourselves taking his bowl and setting out a seat
you leave the Deer Park before he arrives
games.why: the Vinaya says they couldn't keep the pact. one took his bowl and robe, one set a seat, one brought water for his feet.

practice: Settle the breath, then slowly say the four truths, inwardly or in a low voice: there is suffering; suffering has a cause, craving; suffering can end; there is a path to its ending.
Take a full breath between each one, and if one slips from memory, that's fine; start again. Then rest in the quiet after the last one.

wordCard.voice: Asalha again. The full moon when Theravada Buddhists remember the first sermon in the Deer Park: the middle way, the four truths, and the wheel set rolling. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali dhammacakka: the wheel of the teaching, set rolling in the first sermon.

carryVoice: Your line: the wheel, again. Whatever arises, ceases, as Kondanna saw. That's today, done.
